title: Re: Ask HN: What AI tools help me understand a MR?...
text:
Check out the branch, run the code locally, read it, ask claude code or codex or whatever harness to explain things you don't understand. Ask it to diagram the code boundaries and modules and model the system so you can visually understand it.

use AI to write smoke tests without access to the code i.e. first describe something a correct implementation should do with only the knowledge of the interface not the implementation, and run the tests to see if it behaves the way you think it should.

title: Re: Claude Duet...
text:
Powered by Opus 5.5 is incredible.

I've been using ChatGPT Dot over Meta Muse/Instinct/Grok Bot because it's been powered by Astra and I find having a personal assistant that's using a true frontier model makes a huge difference in how much I can just trust the output without doing the work again myself just to double check the results.

In the past month since Dot came out, I've literally bought a car with almost the entire process handled by Dot, and am now in the process of buying a house in Kyoto, in a language I don't speak at all, coordinating with an obscene amount of moving parts and logistics, flawlessly handled entirely by Dot, from finding the home to scheduling visits with real estate agents to finding judicial scriveners and getting a hanko stamp and scheduling inspections and applying for insurance and all sorts of insane tasks that would have taken infinitely longer and been unbelievably painful on my own.

So, so excited to see what Duet looks like with Opus 5.5. Going to try switching over as soon as I get off the waitlist.

Curious how other people have found these agents as well - always love hearing and seeing what other people have done with these things and how to improve my flow even better. I feel like I'm very close to being able to essentially offload every single task I do on a computer to an agent like this.

title: Re: Mine Rogue. Vibe-coded balatro-inspired minesweepe...
text:
Hey folks!

First time sharing something here. I've been vibe-coding a browser game inspired in Balatro.

It's a minesweeper game where you play rounds of increasing difficulty. At the end of each round you can buy different bonuses that do special things like "reveal a random safe tile after every 5th successful move".

The game was done using Claude Opus 5.5. In a previous version I had a screenshot test suite that took 15 minutes to run, I burned the whole project to the ground and started again.

Behind the hook, I instructed Claude to use React, and I know it uses 98.css (https://jdan.github.io/98.css/) and the icons from 95.css (https://win98icons.alexmeub.com/).

It's the first time I share something I "made" without reading absolutely any of the code.

Hope you find it entertaining, or at least that it brings back some nostalgia for simpler times.

title: Re: Show HN: Built Taskman, a Rust TUI for Parallel Cl...
text:
Most of my time building feels like a dance across (i) Claude/Codex TUIs (ii) Github PRs and (iii) Jira/Linear/etc issues. The greater the parallelization, the more intricate the dance feels. At some point, parallel work on N issues leads to 3*N windows. OS window management starts to feel cumbersome and ultimately constraining. You can go a bit further with things like using different desktops, one per project, and at least only seeing the windows of one project at a time.

I’ve looked into agent orchestration tools like Herdr, Emdash, Conductor, Superset but felt features most useful to me were spread across them. Herdr is built more around agents and panes and less around issues. The rest may come closer with linking PRs and issues, but they’re desktop apps. Claude Code’s agent view is good for hopping between sessions, but it doesn’t currently address the window overload problem.

My preference for the Claude/Codex TUIs over the desktop versions nudged me to explore what blend of the two I can get away with. This led to a Rust shell where the issue and PR sit beside a Claude/Codex session. It’s a TUI with its prefix key etc. that also supports less traditionally-TUI things like drag-to-reorder for projects/issues. It’s a Claude/Codex++ designed around multiple sessions and minimizing chasing windows or alt-tabbing. Ultimately, it remains an extension over my Claude/Codex TUI experience and helps with the multitasking dance across different live threads. Curious if this approach or even problem statement resonates with others.

Happy to answer questions and feedback is very welcome!

title: Show HN: Jev drives a browser – HN login and search in 8s for half a cent
text:
I put this repo and site together as an educational reference for folks getting started with Jev / OpenAI Decisions API.

This demonstrates how Jev can drive a browser (the idea being extract it into a skills file). On every step the page's controls are extracted into a table, and Jev picks an operation and a target, with a probability for every option.

Try the HN login replay (https://jev-browser.rovira.sh/#hackernews-login), Amazon (https://jev-browser.rovira.sh/#amazon-cart), or run it live with your own key.

Interesting bits: - Jev mean response time is 250ms (123–495 ms on the HN run). - Jev never sees the DOM, only a table of controls extracted from it ahead of time. It's in some ways, similar to the accessibility tree that good LLM browser skills use now. - Jev can't generate text (in a good way) so this need to be provided ahead of time, either by you or a complementary LLM. - Each step is stateless and costs a few thousand input tokens, under a tenth of a cent.

Repo (three files, no dependencies): https://github.com/zurfyx/jev-browser-skill

title: Re: Elektric – Benchmark your AI requests across 150 m...
text:
Hi all,

I built Elektric to solve a widespread problem in AI today: people pick models based on vibes, not data.

Elektric Benchmark collects 1000 representative requests from your AI app and evaluates them across 150 models to compare your current setup on quality and cost. The key difference from public benchmarks is that Elektric compares your actual AI traffic.

From there, Elektric can do two things with that information.

Elektric Grid is our automatic router. Your AI app sends us a request and we pick which model should handle it based on the request's characteristics and difficulty. Simply, not all requests need a frontier model. Many requests can be answered by capable but cheaper models like Luna. To use Grid, you simply change the base URL and API key of your OpenAI-compatible SDK, or use our SDK, and begin sending requests with "model: elektric-grid".

Elektric Wire - users that want to choose their own model can access 150+ models from all leading providers through one API and one account balance without maintaining integrations with multiple providers.

Some useful links: - The AI Model Should Disappear: https://elektric.ai/blog/the-ai-model-should-disappear - Why We Built Elektric on Cloudflare: https://elektric.ai/blog/why-we-built-elektric-on-cloudflare - How Elektric Determines Quality for Benchmarks: https://elektric.ai/blog/how-elektric-determines-quality-for...

I am interested in people trying it and telling me where it breaks, whether something is confusing, and most importantly, how useful is the benchmark idea actually. All questions and comments are welcome here or on vasileios@elektric.ai

title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
text:
My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it.

Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team.

So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions.

In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed.

Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide.

Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction.

Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much.

You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki.

Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?
